title: The 10 Best Bar Clamps
subtitle: Quick-grip trigger clamps, steel F-clamps and parallel clamps for glue-ups and assembly, ranked from live Amazon data.
intro: Clamps are the tool you never have enough of. We ranked 10 best-selling bar clamp sets on rating, review volume and features (600 lbs or more of force, 24-inch or longer capacity, parallel jaws and spreader conversion). There are three types: one-handed trigger clamps for quick holds and light glue-ups (about 150 lbs), steel F-clamps for real pressure (400-600 lbs), and parallel clamps that stay square on cabinets and panels (1,100 lbs and up). Sets run from about $24 for two WORKPRO 12-inch clamps to $200 for Bora's four parallel clamps.
data_source: Amazon product listings on the data_captured date. Prices, ratings and review counts change daily; check the listing before relying on a number.

avoid.name: 4 Inch Bar Clamps for Woodworking, 5 Pcs Trigger Quick Grip Clamps, One Handed Ratchet
avoid.flag: No clamping force listed; specs are placeholders
avoid.verdict: Five tiny clamps with nothing on the listing to tell you what they can hold. The WORKPRO pair costs more but lists 150 lbs and has 5,795 reviews.
reasons: The listing never gives a clamping force, the one number that tells you what a clamp can do. Every other set here states one.
The spec table lists the model number as '1' and the weight of five clamps as 0.01 kg (about a third of an ounce). Neither can be right.
It calls them 'heavy-duty' and 'c clamps' as well as bar clamps, so the listing can't settle on what you're buying.

buyers_guide.q: Which type of clamp do I need?
buyers_guide.a: Trigger clamps (Quick-Grip style) are fast and one-handed, but only about 150 lbs, fine for holding work and light glue-ups. Steel F-clamps reach 400-600 lbs for real glue joints. Parallel clamps apply 1,000+ lbs with jaws that stay parallel, which keeps cabinets and panels square.

buyers_guide.q: How many clamps do I need?
buyers_guide.a: More than you think. A typical panel glue-up uses a clamp every 8 to 12 inches, alternating above and below. Start with four to six of the size you use most.

buyers_guide.q: What size clamps should I buy?
buyers_guide.a: 6 and 12-inch clamps for small parts and edge work, 24 to 36-inch for tabletops, frames and cabinet sides. The listed size is the maximum opening; check throat depth (reach) too.

buyers_guide.q: What does converting to a spreader mean?
buyers_guide.a: Many clamps let you reverse the fixed jaw so the clamp pushes outward. That's useful for separating glued parts or pressing assemblies apart.
Steel jaws can dent softwood and stain wood with glue. Use the built-in pads, or put scrap blocks between the jaws and the work.
